Survival analysis studies the time until an event happens: death, relapse, machine failure, customer
churn, or any other well-defined endpoint. What makes this kind of data special, and what separates
survival analysis from ordinary regression, is that we usually cannot observe the event time for
everyone. Some subjects are still event-free when the study ends, some drop out early, and some
enter late. Handling these partially observed times correctly is the entire point of the field, and
it starts with how you represent the data.

This page explains the structure of survival data, introduces the `Surv` object (the response type
that every estimator and model in Greenwood consumes), and shows how to describe a response by
column names when your data lives in a data frame.

## Why survival data is different

Imagine a study that follows patients for two years and records the time until relapse. At the end
of the study, three situations are possible for any given patient.

The first is a fully observed event: the patient relapsed at a known time, say 8 months. The second
is right censoring: the patient was relapse-free at their last visit, say at 20 months, so all we
know is that their true relapse time is greater than 20 months. The third is a variation on
censoring caused by how subjects enter and leave the study.

Right censoring is by far the most common situation, and it is why we cannot simply average the
observed times or run a standard regression on them. A censored time of 20 months is not the same as
an event at 20 months, and treating it as one would badly bias every estimate. Survival methods are
built to use the partial information in a censored observation without pretending it is a complete
one.

::: {#fig-censoring}

still event-free at month 20, so their true event time is only known to exceed 20: this is right
censoring.

Greenwood also supports less common but important patterns: left censoring (the event happened
before a known time), interval censoring (the event happened between two known times), and left
truncation or late entry (a subject only becomes observable after some delay). All of these are
expressed through the same response object.

::: {.callout-note}
## The key idea

A survival observation carries two pieces of information: a time, and a status that says what the
time means (an event, or a censoring point). You must always keep them together. Greenwood does this
for you with the `Surv` object.
:::

## The Surv object

`Surv` is the response you pass to estimators and models. It bundles the times with their status
codes, so that downstream code can rely on a clean, consistent representation. You build one with a
single call, `gw.Surv(time, time2, event, type=, origin=)`, which mirrors R's `survival::Surv()`
argument for argument. As in R, the kind of response is inferred from the arguments you supply.

The most common case is right-censored data: pass the observed times and an event indicator, where a
true value (or `1`) means the event occurred and a false value (or `0`) means the observation was
censored.

```{python}
# Import the Greenwood library
import greenwood as gw

# Four subjects: events at 5 and 4, censored at 6 and 9
y = gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4, 9], event=[1, 0, 1, 0])

# Display a compact summary of the response
y
```

The `repr` gives a quick summary: the censoring type, the number of observations, and how many of
them were events. You can also reach the derived quantities directly.

```{python}
# Read off the derived counts directly from the response
print("observations:", y.n)
print("events:", y.n_events)
print("censored:", y.n_censored)
```

### Other censoring types

When subjects enter the risk set after time zero, or when a covariate changes during follow-up, you
use the counting-process form. Each observation is an interval `(start, stop]` with an event
indicator at the stop time. This is also how left truncation is expressed. Supplying `time2=` is all
it takes: `time` becomes the start and `time2` the stop.

```{python}
# Each row is an interval (start, stop] with an event indicator at the stop time
gw.Surv(time=[0, 2, 1], time2=[5, 6, 4], event=[1, 0, 1])
```

The remaining types must be requested explicitly with `type=`, exactly as in R. With
`type="left"`, a status of `1` is an exact event and a status of `0` means the event had already
happened by the recorded time (left censoring).

```{python}
# Status 1 is an exact event, status 0 is left-censored at the recorded time
gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4], event=[1, 0, 1], type="left")
```

Interval censoring, where the event is known only to fall between two times, is most easily written
with `type="interval2"`. The two times are the lower and upper bounds. An upper bound of
`numpy.inf` (or a missing value) marks right censoring, a missing lower bound marks left censoring,
and equal bounds mark an exact event. R's other form, `type="interval"`, takes the two times plus a
status code (`0` right, `1` exact, `2` left, `3` interval) and is supported too.

```{python}
import numpy as np

# The event is known only to fall in [lower, upper]; numpy.inf marks right censoring
gw.Surv(time=[1, 2, 3], time2=[2, np.inf, 5], type="interval2")
```

Competing risks and multi-state endpoints, where more than one kind of event can occur, follow R's
rule as well: make the event a categorical. The first category means censoring, and the remaining
categories are the states, in order.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

# The first category ("censor") is censoring, and the others are the states
outcome = pd.Categorical(
    ["relapse", "death", "censor", "relapse"],
    categories=["censor", "relapse", "death"],
)
gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 7, 8], event=outcome)
```

When each endpoint lives in its own time and event columns instead, `gw.first_event()` builds the
same multi-state response by taking the earliest event per subject. The [competing
risks](13-competing-risks.qmd) page shows it in action.

## Building a response from a data frame

Greenwood offers two layers for building a response. `gw.Surv()`, which mirrors R's
`survival::Surv()`, and `gw.event_time()` build a response from values you already hold: lists,
NumPy arrays, or simulated data, as in the examples above. When your data lives in a data frame,
you describe the response instead, by column names and expressions. A formula such as
`"Surv(time, status == 2) ~ age"` or an outcome such as
`gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status == 2")` names the columns, and the estimator evaluates
it against the frame you pass as `data=` when it fits. Because the description holds names rather
than data frame code, it works the same on every backend (pandas, Polars, PyArrow, DuckDB, and lazy
frames). That is why it is the recommended way to start from a data frame.

The bundled `lung` dataset, from the North Central Cancer Treatment Group, is a good example.

```{python}
# Load the bundled lung dataset as a Polars DataFrame
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars")

# Preview the raw data
lung
```

In this dataset, and in several others that come from R, the `status` column is coded `1` for
censored and `2` for dead, rather than the `0`/`1` convention. `Surv()` handles this the way R does:
when the largest status value is `2`, the codes are read as `1`/`2` and shifted down to `0`/`1`. So
the column passes straight through, and the formula is the one you would write in R.

```{python}
# The response and the covariates in one R-style formula, evaluated against `data=`
gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex", data=lung)
```

### Describing an outcome once

When you fit several models to the same endpoint, or a model that takes no covariates, describe the
response once with `gw.Outcome.surv()`. It takes the same arguments as `Surv()`, each written as it
would be inside a formula, and holds no data.

```{python}
# The lung endpoint, described by column names
death = gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status")
death
```

Pass it to any estimator along with `data=`. Covariates and grouping arguments such as `by=` or
`strata=` can then be column names too:

```{python}
# The same description drives a Kaplan-Meier curve and a Cox model
km = gw.KaplanMeier().fit(death, by="sex", data=lung)
cox = gw.CoxPH().fit(death, covariates=["age", "sex", "ph.ecog"], data=lung)
cox
```

Binding at fit time reads every column the model uses from the one frame, and it drops any row with
a missing value in one of them, as R's `na.omit` does. The response and the covariates therefore can
never get out of step. The printout reports how many rows were dropped, and the fitted model keeps
the count in `n_dropped_`. Here, one patient has no `ph.ecog` score.

A formula's response parses to the same `Outcome`, and `bind()` evaluates either one against a
frame when you want the `Surv` itself.

```{python}
# The formula response and the Outcome are the same description
print(gw.Outcome.from_formula(formula="Surv(time, status)") == death)

# Bind the description to a frame to get a Surv
death.bind(lung)
```

### The expression grammar

Each argument of a response is a column name or an expression. The expressions mirror what you
would write in R, so a formula copied from an R script usually works unchanged. For any status
coding other than `0`/`1` or `1`/`2`, write a comparison that gives a true or false value per row.
The `pbc` dataset codes `status` as `0` (censored), `1` (transplant), and `2` (dead). This column
must not be passed raw, because R's rules would read it as a `1`/`2` coding and mark the `0` rows as
invalid. An all-cause endpoint and a death-only endpoint are each one comparison:

```{python}
# Load the pbc dataset, whose status has three levels (0, 1, 2)
pbc = gw.load_dataset("pbc", backend="polars")

# All-cause: anything other than 0 is an event
print("all-cause: ", gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status != 0").bind(pbc))

# Death only: transplant becomes censoring
print("death-only:", gw.Outcome.surv(time="time", event="status == 2").bind(pbc))
```

The comparisons are `==`, `!=`, `in`, and `not in`. R's `status %in% c(1, 2)` is accepted as a
spelling of `status in (1, 2)`. Strings are compared the same way, which saves recoding an outcome
column by hand. Missing values follow R: `==` and `!=` with a missing value give a missing status,
while `in` gives false.

```{python}
import polars as pl

# Build a small example with string outcomes
study = pl.DataFrame({
    "time": [12.0, 5.5, 20.0, 8.0],
    "outcome": ["died", "withdrew", "censored", "died"],
})

# Only "died" is an event, and the other outcomes are censored
gw.KaplanMeier().fit("Surv(time, outcome == 'died') ~ 1", data=study)
```

For competing risks and multi-state endpoints, R's `factor(x, levels, labels)` turns a status
column into a categorical. The first label means censored and the remaining labels are the states,
in order. R's ranges such as `0:2` work for the levels, and repeating a label merges levels (for
example, two codes that both mean censored).

```{python}
# pbc as a competing-risks response: transplant and death are separate states
gw.Outcome.surv(
    time="time",
    event="factor(status, c(0, 1, 2), c('censor', 'transplant', 'death'))",
).bind(pbc)
```

A time can also be computed from two date columns with `duration(start, end, unit=)`, where the
unit is `"days"` (the default), `"weeks"`, `"months"`, or `"years"`. The
[Data sources](04-data-sources.qmd) page shows it on a study export.

On the right-hand side of a formula, `strata()`, `cluster()`, and `frailty()` terms route columns to
the `strata=`, `cluster=`, and `frailty_cluster=` arguments. For the non-parametric estimators and
the hypothesis tests, the right-hand side names the grouping column(s).

```{python}
# A formula for a stratified Cox model, a grouped Kaplan-Meier curve, and the log-rank test
gw.CoxPH().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex + strata(inst)", data=lung)
km = gw.KaplanMeier().fit("Surv(time, status) ~ sex", data=lung)
gw.logrank_test("Surv(time, status) ~ sex", data=lung)
```

A formula's response and the arguments of an `Outcome` only ever name columns and literal values.
Nothing in them is evaluated as Python code.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Check your event coding

The event must be logical, `0`/`1`, or `1`/`2`. Any other value is not an error: following R, it
becomes a missing status and Greenwood issues a warning ("Invalid status value, converted to NA").
Missing rows are dropped when you fit. Watch for that warning, since it usually means a column with
more than two codes was used without a comparison. The section on
[missing values and validation](#missing-values-and-validation) shows what happens next.
:::

### Writing it as an event-time vector

Sometimes the clearest way to describe a censored time is to say what kind it is. `gw.event_time()`
does exactly that. It is a port of Max Kuhn's etd R package, and it pairs each time with a
one-letter status: `"e"` for an exact event, `"r"` for right-censored,
`"l"` for left-censored, and `"i"` for interval-censored. For interval-censored values, `time_max=`
holds the upper end of the interval.

```{python}
# One exact, one right-censored, one left-censored, and one interval-censored time
x = gw.event_time(
    time=[7, 5, 3, 2],
    status=["e", "r", "l", "i"],
    time_max=[None, None, None, 4],
)
x
```

The printout uses the familiar notation: `5+` is right-censored, `3-` is left-censored, and `[2, 4]`
is an interval. Convert to a `Surv` with `gw.as_surv()` when you need one.

```{python}
# Convert the event-time vector to the equivalent Surv
gw.as_surv(x)
```

You often do not need the conversion at all, because estimators accept an event-time vector
directly.

```{python}
# Turnbull's NPMLE fitted straight from the event-time vector
gw.Turnbull().fit(x)
```

When the times and codes are columns of a frame, describe them by name with
`gw.Outcome.event_time(time=, status=, time_max=)` or the formula response
`event_time(time, status, time_max)`, just as with `Surv`.

## Missing values and validation

`Surv()` follows R in how it treats questionable input. It does not reject a row outright. Instead,
an invalid status code becomes a missing value with a warning, and missing times or statuses are
kept in the response. The `repr` reports how many rows are missing, and every estimator drops them
when it fits, as R's `na.omit` does, and reports the count.

```{python}
# The status of 3 is invalid, so the last row becomes missing
y = gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 7, 8, 9], event=[1, 0, 1, 1, 3])

# The missing row is dropped at fit time, and the printout says so
gw.KaplanMeier().fit(y)
```

The counting-process form has one more rule from R. Each start must be strictly less than its stop.
A row where a subject enters and exits at the same time has no time at risk, so `Surv()` sets its
start to missing with the warning "Stop time must be > start time, NA created".

```{python}
# Subject 1 enters at time 1 and exits at time 1 (zero follow-up), so the row becomes missing
gw.Surv(time=[1, 0], time2=[1, 2], event=[1, 0])
```

If you see this warning, check your data:

- **Most common fix**: exclude subjects with `start >= stop` (they have zero or negative follow-up
time)
- **Data quality check**: why do some subjects have identical entry and exit times? Is this a data
entry error?
- **If intentional**: if the event truly occurred instantaneously, add a small epsilon to the stop
time: `stop = start + 1e-10`

## Serialization

A response also serializes to and from JSON without loss, which is useful for saving an analysis
input or moving it between systems. Calling `to_json()` returns a plain string, so you can write it
to a file or send it over the wire. Here is the serialized form of the `lung` response, truncated to
its first stretch so you can see the shape of it.

```{python}
# Load data and bind the lung response to get a Surv
lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars")
y = death.bind(lung)

# Serialize the response to a self-contained JSON string
text = y.to_json(indent=None)

# Peek at the first 200 characters to see the structure
text[:200]
```

That string carries the times and status codes together, which is exactly what a `Surv` object
holds. Reading it back with `from_json()` reconstructs an equivalent response, and we can confirm
nothing was lost by comparing the JSON of the original and the restored object.

```{python}
# Reconstruct an equivalent response from the JSON string
restored = gw.Surv.from_json(text)

# Confirm the round-trip preserved every value
print("round-trips exactly:", restored.to_json() == y.to_json())
```

For working in memory rather than as text, `to_dict()` and `from_dict()` perform the same round-trip
with a plain Python dictionary, and `to_frame()` (optionally with a `format=` of `"polars"`,
`"pandas"`, or `"pyarrow"`) gives a tidy, one-row-per-subject view that is convenient for inspection
or export.

```{python}
# Export as a tidy one-row-per-subject DataFrame for inspection or export
y.to_frame(format="polars")
```

The dictionary form is the same structure `to_json()` serializes, so `gw.Surv.from_dict()` rebuilds
an equivalent response from it.

```{python}
# Serialize to a dict, then immediately reconstruct from it
gw.Surv.from_dict(gw.Surv(time=[5, 6, 4], event=[1, 0, 1]).to_dict())
```

## The risk-set table

Under every non-parametric estimate is one tabulation: at each distinct event time, how many
subjects are still at risk, how many have the event, and how many are censored. This risk-set table
is what Kaplan-Meier, the log-rank test, and Cox all build on, and you can compute it directly with
`event_table()`. It matches R's `survfit` tabulation.

```{python}
# Tabulate events and censorings at each distinct event time
gw.event_table(death, data=lung).to_frame(format="polars")
```

Each row is a distinct time. The `n_risk` column counts the subjects under observation just before
that time, `n_event` the events at it, and `n_censor` the censorings. Name a grouping column on the
right-hand side of a formula (or pass `group=`) to tabulate within strata, which adds a `strata`
column.

```{python}
# Tabulate separately within each level of the `sex` column
gw.event_table("Surv(time, status) ~ sex", data=lung).to_frame(format="polars")
```

You rarely need this table directly, but it is the shared foundation the estimators are built on,
and it is handy when you want to check counts by hand or drive a custom calculation.
